Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01209

But the argument usually given for this view shows that its supporters have accepted it without a sound basis. They say that if souls were empty of these acts of understanding, that emptiness would either be essential or accidental. If it were essential, the soul could never understand anything. An essential feature cannot disappear. If the emptiness were a passing feature, it could only happen to a soul whose understanding is essential. So the soul’s understanding of things must be essential to it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01210

This argument is extremely weak. It assumes that the absence of knowledge must either be essential or accidental, as if these were the only two options. It also treats things that are not opposites as though they were. The fact that knowledge is not essential to the soul does not mean that the absence of knowledge is essential to it. We are not saying that the soul requires knowledge never to exist. We are saying only that it does not require knowledge to exist. The soul can gain knowledge if the cause of that knowledge is present. If the cause is absent, the knowledge will not be there. But not everything that is absent must be impossible; otherwise every possible thing would always be absent.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01211

If knowledge were essential to the soul, it would never be separated from it. The supporters of this view say that souls understand intelligible forms, but their attachment to the body and complete absorption in managing it keep them from noticing their own inner state. This cannot be right. Either the intelligible forms are actually present in the soul or they are not. If they are present, the soul must be aware of them, since the presence of one immaterial thing to another is awareness. If they are not actually present, then knowledge is not essential to the soul.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01212

They might say that these forms are stored in the soul as in a storehouse. But to say this is to say that the soul has the ability to recover them by connecting with that storehouse. That ability is acquired only through earlier acts of understanding. If merely having the forms in an intellectual being—such as the Active Intellect—and being able to connect with them were enough to count as understanding, then every soul would already know everything in the Active Intellect in this sense. This would bring us back to the symbolic interpretation just described. There is an obvious difference between knowing something in act and having the potential to know it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01213
XXXVI. Learning is not recollection
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01214

The claim that learning is recollection is closer to the truth than the claim just discussed. Some careful thinkers who believed souls existed before bodies saw that knowledge could not be essential to the soul. They therefore said that before joining the body, souls knew all things. This knowledge was not essential, so it disappeared when the soul became absorbed in managing the body. On this view, thinking is a kind of remembering, and learning is recollection.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01215

They support this view by saying that thought is a search. But it is impossible to search for something wholly unknown, and impossible to search for something already known. When someone finds what he was looking for, he recognizes it as the thing he sought. For example, when a runaway servant is found, the master recognizes that this is the same servant who ran away. If knowledge were not already present before the search, it would be impossible to seek and acquire it. If, instead, the knowledge had been there all along and thinking were recollection, then the thinker would recognize the answer as the thing he had been looking for.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01216

The answer is that the proof that the soul comes into being will be given later. Their argument is a familiar puzzle discussed near the beginning of books on logic, where its solution is also explained. Every statement has a subject, a predicate, and a relation between them. When we seek to know a statement, we do not seek to understand its subject, its predicate, or the relation between them. We seek to establish that the relation holds or does not hold—that is, to judge whether the predicate belongs to the subject. Once thought leads us to accept or reject the statement, we know that we have found what we were seeking. We knew the parts of the statement as ideas, but we did not know whether the statement was true. The parts were already understood; the judgment we sought was not yet acquired. The same applies when we seek to understand a concept.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01217

What we acquire through thought is not the same as what we knew before we began. Each thing we seek has a sign by which we can recognize it once we find it. The seeker knows that it is the answer because it matches that sign. The author of The Summary offers a strong objection about acquiring concepts. By God’s help, I have untangled and answered it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01218
XXXVII. Why intelligible forms are not in bodies or bodily powers
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01219

If what we know is an intelligible form, no bodily power, or any power in a body, can perceive it. Here is the proof. Any image perceived by a power in a body must either exist in that body or not exist in it. If it does exist there, it is not an intelligible form but a sensible one. We assumed it was intelligible, so that cannot be right.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01220

If it does not exist in the body where the perceiving power is, then the material basis of that power must have a spatial relation to it. We have established that bodily powers can act and be acted on only through such a relation. If a bodily power could act or be acted on without matter and its position, it would exist without matter. For existence comes before either acting or being acted on, and both depend on something's existing first. Any power that does something by its own being, rather than through its matter, must be self-subsisting. It would be free of matter in its nature and in its awareness.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01221

But we assumed that the perceiving power was bodily. If it perceived the image, the image would have to occupy a position in relation to the body where that power exists. The image itself would therefore have a position. Anything with a position is divisible, either actually or potentially.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01222

If its parts were alike, then the same intelligible thing would be understood not once, but potentially an infinite number of times. If the parts differed, some would have to serve as the broader kind and others as the defining features that complete the form. For when a thing's parts are not parts of its measured size, they must be parts of its meaning. Its meaning would then be made up of different meanings. A thing's meaning can be divided only into broader kind and defining features.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01223

But if these parts of meaning line up with parts of size, there can be different ways to divide the size. Suppose we first divide it into a broader kind and a particular defining feature. If we divide it another way, either we find the same broader kind and defining feature again, which is impossible, or we find a new broader kind and defining feature. Then the thing would acquire essential parts it did not have before. But the parts that make up a thing must come before it in the order of its nature. A division can reveal those parts; it cannot create them. Since a size can be divided endlessly, this would give one thing endlessly many broader kinds and defining features. That is impossible.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01224

There is another problem. Why should the image on one side be the broader kind and the image on another side the defining feature? If the act of imagining a division creates this distinction, imagining would change the thing's form and nature. That is impossible. If the distinction were already there, then we would be understanding two things, not one. The same question would arise for each, and we would end up understanding infinitely many things whenever we understand one.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01225

How, then, could two intelligible meanings make up one intelligible thing? We understand the nature of the broader kind as the same in the nature of the defining feature. They are parts that can both be said of the whole, and predication means that they are one in existence. How could a bodily sign point to one of them in one place and to the other somewhere else, as happens with parts that are separate in position? The form and nature of the defining feature would have to be present in the body wherever the form and nature of the broader kind were. The defining feature of blackness, for example, is that it constricts the eye; this feature is present in the very place where blackness is. This makes it clear that true intelligible forms cannot exist in bodies or bodily matter.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01226

You might object: Aren't blackness, whiteness, animals, trees, and other material things intelligible to us? They exist in matter and can be divided by size. Does that not mean that a divided thing, precisely as divided, can be understood?
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01227

We reply that being divisible by size belongs to these things because of how they exist outside the mind. Their being divisible, either in themselves or through something else, is part of their material mode of existence. Their existence in the intellect is different. In that mode, they cannot be divided by position.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01228

This puzzle is especially hard to solve for those who think understanding means stripping an essence of its extra features. Some things have bodily extension and divisibility as part of their definition. An animal or a sphere, for example, remains divisible actually or potentially even after its incidental features are stripped away. If an essence keeps all its essential features in every mode of existence, then it seems that an intelligible animal or sphere must also be divisible. That makes the problem seem even harder.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01229

On our account, a thing's essence is its meaning or concept. Take corporeality: its meaning is “a substance that can have dimensions.” This meaning exists outside the mind, and it also exists in the mind. When the meaning of corporeality exists in the mind, it exists in a different way. That mental existence carries the concept of corporeality as it is, but it is not itself extended or divisible.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01230

Blackness, too, means “a color that constricts the eye.” When it exists in bodily matter, it has the effects that belong to that kind of existence. When its meaning exists in the intellect, it exists in another way. It carries the meaning of color and of constricting the eye, but it does not make the intellect physically colored or cause it to constrict anyone's sight. If that intellectual existence were present to an intellect, the intellect would understand the meaning of blackness without treating its physical effect as present there.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01231

Things have different kinds of existence, even when their meaning and essence are one. We know the same nature—for example, a human being—through sensation, through imagination, and through intellect. This shows us that one essence can exist materially, purely intellectually, or in an intermediate way.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01232
XXXVIII. The senses do not know that what they perceive exists
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01233

That is the work of the intellect. Sensory perception involves the sense organs being affected and images of the things perceived appearing in them. Some say these images exist in the organs themselves, as most people believe. The truth, however, is that they appear in the soul, which uses the senses as a means of showing them. In either case, this happens because the material sense organ is ready to receive them.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01234

Our hand feels heat because it is ready to be affected by heat. The eye senses a visible image because it is ready for sight; the ear hears a sound because it is ready for hearing. The senses do no more than sense: they receive the image of what is sensed, either in the organ or in the soul through the organ's use. The senses, or the soul insofar as it is sensing, do not know that the thing sensed exists outside them. We learn this through experience. That is the work of the intellect, or the reasoning soul, not of the senses or imagination.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01235

Here is proof. A person who is out of his mind may see images in the shared inner sense that have no existence outside him. He may ask, “What are these things I see?” or say, “I see so-and-so,” and be certain that what he sees is really there. For him, these images are present just as other sensory images are. Since his intellect cannot judge that they have no external existence, he assumes that they are outside him.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01236

The same thing happens in dreams. A sleeper sees, hears, smells, tastes, and touches things that have no real existence outside him, yet is sure that he is experiencing them. Their images are present in imagination and the shared inner sense just as they are in waking life. What is missing is the intellect's ability to reflect and judge what kind of things they are.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01237

Likewise, when our hands feel heat, whether it comes from outside or from an inner bodily imbalance, the senses only register the heat. It is the intellect, through reasoning, that concludes that there must be a hot body, either inside or outside us. When we lift something heavy, we feel its weight and are affected by it. We do not sense that the heaviness comes from an external heavy body; we learn that through experience.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01238

From this, a thoughtful person can see that the soul has another mode of existence beyond the world of material bodies. In that mode, images and qualities can exist without bodily matter to carry them. What we established earlier about sensible qualities helps prove this: the qualities found in our sensory powers are not the very same qualities found in material things. They belong to another kind, the qualities of the soul.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01239

What we hear, see, or touch are sensible qualities that represent things; in reality, they exist in the soul. In the same way, the intellectual forms of material substances—human beings, horses, spheres, stars, water, and fire—are these things as understood, but they exist as intellectual substances, truly united with the intellect in act.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01240
Such claims are among the remarkable things we learn about the human soul and life after death. We will explain them further, God willing.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01241
XXXIX. The kinds of knowledge
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01242

For us, knowledge is a form of existence. Existence has three levels: complete, self-sufficient, and incomplete. The first is the world of pure intellects, forms that are free of dimensions, bodies, and matter. The second is the world of animal souls and imaginal forms. The third is the world of forms that exist in and depend on matter; these are the forms we sense.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01243

The material things themselves, which keep changing and coming into being, are so steeped in nonexistence, possibility, and darkness that they are not properly known in themselves. We do speak of them as existing, as we do time and motion. But, as we have explained, each exists only for a single instant; the instants themselves exist only potentially. Material things endure for one instant and pass away in all the others. Their existence is therefore called existence only figuratively. It is also reasonable to speak of them as not existing. Plato points to this when he asks: “What is it that comes to be but does not truly exist? And what is it that truly exists but does not come to be?”
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01244
By the first he means material things, and by the second, things free of matter.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01245

Strictly speaking, then, there are three worlds, each a kind of knowledge, or knowing form. Some Sufis count four, since they include this world of material things as a kind of existence. They speak of five Divine Presences: the Presence of the Essence, the Names, the Attributes, the Acts, and the Effects. There is no need to dispute the count, as long as we understand that material things have such weak existence that they are not knowing forms in themselves. They are known only through something else.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01246

We can therefore speak of four kinds of possible things. The first are complete in both existence and knowability: the intellects and the forms actually understood. Because their existence is so strong, luminous, and pure, they are free of bodies, images, and number. Though they are many, they exist together in a single, unified existence, with no separation between their realities, for they are all immersed in the Divine. The Qur'an points to this realm in the words, “what you cannot see.” Earlier philosophers called it the Elemental Realm.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01247

The second is the world of the souls of the heavenly spheres, immaterial images, and forms with dimensions. These are self-sufficient, yet they also depend on their intellectual principles. Their connection with the fully existing Divine forms makes up for what they lack and draws them into that higher realm.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01248

The third is the world of sensory souls, the lower spiritual realm, and all the images that are actually perceived through the senses and their organs. These, too, belong to the lower spiritual realm. As long as they remain at this level, their existence is incomplete. They rise beyond it and become free of matter as they follow the human soul's ascent into the world of immaterial images.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01249

The fourth is the world of bodily matter and the forms that flow through it, constantly changing, passing away, and coming to be. These exist somewhere between possibility and actuality, endurance and decay: their endurance is their decay, and their coming together is their separation. Since the purpose of creation is knowledge, those who know can, in principle, be divided into three kinds.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01250

The first are complete by nature, like the separate intellects. The second are self-sufficient but need to be perfected; they do not need an outside source to complete them. These include the souls of the heavenly spheres, and, by nature, the souls of the prophets. Once perfected, the prophets may belong to the first group. The third are incomplete by nature and need help from outside themselves, such as revealed books and messengers.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01251

God created all these kinds, fulfilling every possibility that reason can conceive. The Qur'an points to them in the verses “By those who line up in ranks, then drive forward, then recite the Reminder,” and “By those who glide swiftly, then race ahead, then manage affairs.” The order in the second passage may run in the reverse direction, from effects to causes. Those who glide may be the heavenly spheres, as in “Each floats in its orbit.” Those who race ahead may be their souls. Those who manage affairs may be their intellects, which belong to the realm of Command and exist through God's command, “Be.” Or the words “manage affairs” may refer to the very command that comes from God.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01252

We might also say that there are two worlds: the world of separate intellectual and spiritual beings, and the world of luminous and dark bodies. Since the world of separate beings is the world of knowledge and life, God created within it, corresponding to everything in the world of bodies, an intellectual or imaginal form that is its life and the mirror in which it is seen. The Qur'an alludes to these two worlds when it says, “For whoever fears standing before his Lord, there are two gardens.”
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01253

Plato, the noble philosopher, likewise said that there are two worlds: the world of intellect, which contains intellectual forms, and the world of the senses, which contains sensible images. He called the first the world of Being and the second the world of Becoming. It is also reported that he taught in two ways: one through discipline and direct insight into intellectual truths, the other through teaching and learning by reasoning. The first world's “Being” means that it does not appear to the outer senses, just as the “Becoming” of imaginal forms means that they appear to the inner senses. The intellectual world is the source, foundation, cause, and goal of all other existence. We do not see it because it is too fully present, and the distractions of matter veil it from us. The terms may also point to that world's unity and simplicity, in contrast to the many separate individuals in this world.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01254

The luminous Platonic forms are substances in themselves and in their existence. They are the source of the substances and essences in this world, and the realities of the material things we sense. The proof that supports these forms—and indeed all suspended images—is different from the proof we gave earlier for Platonic forms. It begins from the fact that something sensible exists in the world, such as a human being with its matter and particular features. This is the natural human being. We have also established that a human being exists in imagination with a particular size, shape, and character, even though its matter is not present outside the mind.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01255

The intellect can also understand a human being with all its substance, parts, shapes, and qualities, both essential and incidental. But it understands these in a universal way that can apply to many individuals of the same kind. To understand a thing, the intellect does not have to strip away every feature except its essence. It must strip away its spatial, bodily way of existing, the way that requires it to occupy a direction in the material world.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01256

So the human being exists in nature as a material thing, though in that mode it is neither understood by intellect nor sensed as a mental image; it exists in the shared inner sense and imagination, where it can be sensed; and it exists in the intellect, where it is actually understood. We have shown by decisive proof that the existence of a sensible thing, precisely as sensible, is the very existence of a perceiver, and that the actual existence of an intelligible thing is the existence of an intellectual substance. The knower and the known become one in existence. Since the knower is an immaterial substance, the thing known is also immaterial.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01257

The sensible forms that exist in imagination are likewise the very power of imagination, which must be a substance. What exists as one with a substance must itself be a substance. So the human being has an essential image that exists on its own in the world of images, and an intellectual form that exists on its own in the world of intellects. The same applies to every natural thing, each of which has three modes of existence: intellectual, imaginal, and material.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01258

There can be only one intellectual form of each kind, because the kind has one defining nature. It can multiply only through matter or through outside, accidental causes. But the other two kinds of existence may have many individuals of one kind: natural forms multiply through the changes of matter, while images multiply through the soul's active power. If one human form is stripped of material existence and imaginal appearance, and reaches the intellectual realm, then another human form of the same kind that reaches that realm does not add a second intellectual existence. It is the same existence and the same effect, as are all the forms of the same kind, whether they arrive earlier or later. Even a thousand images of one kind would be one there.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01259

This proof shows that every natural kind, whether it has countless individuals or only one, has an intellectual form that exists in its own right in the Divine intellectual realm. This is Plato's view of the Divine Forms. I doubt that anyone over all these centuries, apart from Plato and perhaps one of his followers, has fully grasped his purpose through proof. Only a single humble and obscure seeker seems to have reached it.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01260
1. Closing discussion: Terms with similar meanings
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01261
The following terms are close in meaning, but they are not all interchangeable.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01262

Perception means reaching or attaining. When the intellect reaches and grasps the nature of something intelligible, that is perception in the sense used here. This matches the word's ordinary meaning. Bodily contact, by contrast, is not true meeting; bodies touch only at their surfaces. Some mystics call this world the realm beyond separation.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01263
Awareness is perception without firm certainty. It is the first, still unsteady stage at which knowledge reaches the intellect. This is why we do not speak of God as “being aware” of something.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01264

Conception is when the intellect has fully grasped a meaning. The word comes from “form.” In ordinary speech, a form is the shape of a body; philosophers use it for several things that share one meaning: what makes a thing actually what it is. In the case of knowledge, the forms of things are their realities and essences.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01265

Retention is the state in which forms received by the intellect have become firmly established, so that if they fade from awareness the intellect can bring them back. Retention stands to perception as acting stands to receiving. It may reflect either two different powers or two levels of one power; the second account is more fitting, since the soul's powers and qualities return to one reality.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01266

Some say that God's knowledge cannot be called retention because retention suggests something became firm after being weak, or because we need to retain only what might be lost. The author rejects this. The Qur'an itself speaks of God's keeping the heavens and earth and of His preserving the Reminder.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01267

God's knowledge is His power, and the whole world is the form of His perfect knowledge. His essence, which is His knowledge, preserves all things. His detailed knowledge preserves itself because it is active, not something passively received. The claim that retention implies a change from weakness to firmness is not established. Nor does the possibility of a thing's loss prevent God's detailed knowledge, preserved in the Highest Pen and the Preserved Tablet, from being called retention.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01268

Remembering begins when an image has disappeared from the intellect and the mind tries to bring it back. Philosophers have said that this requires an intellectual storehouse containing all intelligible forms. They disagree about whether this storehouse is separate from the human soul or connected to it in an intellectual way but hidden from it—either because the soul is occupied with the senses or because its intellect has not yet moved from potential to actual.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01269

Some sharp thinkers, including Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, were troubled by remembering. If the lost image is already known, it is present, and what is present cannot be acquired again. If it is not known, it cannot be brought back, because one cannot seek something one cannot picture. Yet we know that we can look for and recover a memory.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01270

I say that these thinkers were puzzled because they failed to understand existence, the clearest of all things. Al-Razi treated it as an idea formed by the mind. He did not see that one thing can exist in different ways, some fuller than others, or that knowledge itself is a kind of existence, not merely a relation. I admit that the puzzle is harder to solve on our own account, where intellectual understanding occurs as the soul becomes one with the Active Intellect, the form of all things.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01271

But it can be solved. The soul has several levels: sensation, imagination, and intellect. Souls differ in strength and completeness. The strongest can be present to one level without losing another. Others are less complete, and some are so limited that only sensation is present to them, with only a faint trace of imagination.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01272

When a soul of intermediate strength connects with the intellectual realm, it leaves the sensory level and directs the body through some of its natural powers. When it returns to the senses, it is no longer present at its intellectual level, but a faint trace remains, like a weak image. With this trace, and with its still-active ability to recover what it has known, the soul can remember the reality of its own being and the fullness of its intellectual nature.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01273

If the image to be recovered had never been pictured in any way, nor had the soul gained even a close readiness to picture it, then it could not be remembered. But that is not the case at issue. If the soul has pictured it in imagination and acquired the ability to return to its storehouse, then it can remember it. Some have made this question difficult because they assumed that no conception can ever be acquired, whether for the first time through thought or later through memory. We have already answered that mistaken argument.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01274

When a vanished image returns and becomes present again, that is also called memory. If the perception was never preceded by disappearance, it is not called memory. Al-Razi returns to his claim that this problem cannot be solved: if you cannot fully understand memory, though it is one of your own powers and you know you can remember, how can you fully understand what you remember, which seems even farther from you? I reply that God is closer to us than anything else, at the very root of our being. We were created and guided so that we might know Him, reach His generosity, behold His presence, and witness His beauty and majesty. The prophets were sent and the books revealed for this purpose, not to leave people lost and confused.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01275

Recognition has been explained in several ways. Some say it is knowledge of particulars, while knowledge is of universals. Others say recognition is conception, while knowledge is assent or judgment. Those who hold the second view consider recognition a higher degree of knowledge. They say that it is easy to assent to the fact that the things we sense depend on a Necessary Being, but beyond human power to picture the reality of the Necessary Being. On this account, everyone who recognizes knows, but not everyone who knows has reached recognition. A person is called a true knower only after traveling deeply through knowledge, from its starting points to its ends, as far as human ability allows.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01276

Others say that recognition occurs when we perceive something, retain its trace in ourselves, then perceive it again and know that it is what we perceived before. Some people believe that spirits existed from eternity; others say they came before bodies. They identify them with the primordial particles drawn from Adam, who acknowledged God's divinity and lordship. They say that the darkness of bodily life made the spirits forget their Lord. Once freed from the body's darkness, they recognize the One they had known before, and this is why such perception is called recognition.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01277

Understanding is grasping a meaning from someone's words. Making something understood is conveying a meaning through words to a listener. Grasping the point of someone's speech is understanding what the speaker intends. The Qur'an says of some people that they scarcely understand a word. The unbelieving Quraysh, consumed by doubts and desires, could not grasp the truths contained in the Qur'an. That is why God speaks of their failure to understand the purpose for which the Book was revealed.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01278

Intellect has many meanings. In ordinary speech it is the ability to recognize what is useful or harmful, and to distinguish good actions from bad. Theologians use it to mean what reason affirms or denies. Philosophers use it in works on proof, in ethics as practical reason, in discussions of the rational soul and its levels, and in divine science and metaphysics. Some of these meanings have already been explained.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01279

Wisdom also has several meanings. It can refer to any sound knowledge or good action, though it is more often used for practical knowledge than theoretical knowledge. It can also mean doing something well or skillfully. God's wisdom is creating what benefits people and looking after their interests, now and in the future. The same can be said of human wisdom.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01280

Some define wisdom as knowing things. This suggests that knowledge of particulars, which continually change, is not itself a perfection; knowledge of realities and essences is lasting and protected from change. The Qur'an calls this the Mother of the Book. Others define wisdom as doing what will have a good outcome, or as following the Creator's example in governing our lives as far as human ability allows.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01281

The philosophers say wisdom is becoming like God in knowledge and action, as far as human beings can. A person should work to keep knowledge free of ignorance, action free of injustice, generosity free of both stinginess and waste, desire free of both excess and weakness, anger free of rashness and cowardice, patience free of laziness and reckless boldness, modesty free of shamelessness and withdrawal, and love free of both excess and neglect. In short, a person should stay on God's path, fulfilling both God's rights and the rights of creation.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01282

Reasoned knowledge is knowledge reached by a method: setting out premises and thinking them through. The word originally referred to tracking game, and for that reason some say it cannot be applied to God, who does not reason by thought or method.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01283

The mind is the soul's ability to acquire knowledge it does not yet have. Mental existence is not the same as the existence of the mind itself. The mind exists in the outside world; what exists in it as a likeness of something outside is said to have mental existence. That means it exists in the mind without producing the effects it would have outside.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01284

God created the human spirit with no knowledge already present in it, as the Qur'an says: “God brought you out of your mothers' wombs knowing nothing.” But He created it for knowledge and worship: “I did not create jinn and human beings except to worship Me.” If the human spirit had not been created to know the realities of things, it would have begun with one of them already present in act, rather than being empty of all of them—just as prime matter, created to receive all natural forms, begins as pure potentiality with no bodily form.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01285

The human spirit, too, begins as pure potentiality, without intelligible forms. Yet it is made to know all realities and connect with them. Knowing God, His realm, and His signs is the goal; worship is the way to draw near to Him and travel toward Him. Worship is also made possible by knowledge and results from it, as in the verse “Establish prayer in remembrance of Me.” Knowledge is at once the beginning and the end, the starting point and the goal. The soul must therefore be able to acquire these forms of knowledge; that readiness is what we call the mind.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01286

Thought is the soul's movement from ideas and judgments already present in it toward what it does not yet know. There is no reason to limit thought to judgments, as some have done. One of Avicenna's books compares thinking to prayer: both are ways of seeking a gift from God. When the rational power longs for an intellectual form, it naturally turns toward the Giver. If the form comes through direct insight, no further work is needed. Otherwise, the soul turns to other powers that prepare it to receive the form by bringing it into likeness with what is present in the world of intellectual forms. In this way, it may reach through effort what it did not reach through direct insight, as in the verse, “He taught you what you did not know.”
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01287

Direct insight is the sudden finding of a middle point that connects the two sides of something unknown. Without that middle point, thought cannot complete a proof or give a definition. The soul in its ignorance is like someone in deep darkness: it needs a guide or a window to light the next step. That window is the middle point, found all at once. The soul's readiness to find such a point directly is called insight.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01288

Intelligence is the strength and completeness of this direct insight. At its highest it is the sacred power described in the Qur'an: “Its oil would almost shine, even if no fire touched it.” The word also suggests pressing forward and quickly recognizing what is true.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01289

Alertness is noticing something someone intended to point out. The word is often used for solving riddles and puzzles. A thought that comes to mind is the soul's movement toward a proof. Strictly speaking, it is the idea that comes to mind, but the soul is called the thinker because it is the place where the idea appears.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01290

Estimation can mean a belief that is more likely false than true. It can also mean judging particular, non-sensible things about particular bodies, as when a young lamb judges its mother to be a friend and a wolf to be an enemy. The word also names the power that makes such judgments. In our view, this estimating power is not a substance separate from intellect and imagination. It is the intellect directed toward an imagined or sensed form. Its judgments are intelligible meanings attached to particular sensible or imagined things. When the soul turns to itself, it becomes intellect free of estimation and of any relation to bodies; when imagined meanings are corrected and their attachments removed, they become pure intelligibles. Estimation is simply the intellect's way of turning toward and being affected by a body, and an estimated thing is an intelligible meaning attached to particular matter.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01291

Opinion is a belief that is more likely true than false. It has degrees of strength. At the strongest end it may be called knowledge; in turn, knowledge may sometimes be called opinion. This is how interpreters understand the Qur'anic phrase “they are certain that they will meet their Lord.” They offer two explanations. First, the knowledge of most people in this life is like opinion when compared with the knowledge of people in the next life. Second, true knowledge in this life is reached only by prophets and the truthful, who are described as those “who believe in God and His Messenger and then do not doubt.”
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01292

Knowledge of certainty, vision of certainty, and truth of certainty are three levels. The first is assent to general truths established by proof, like a blind person's knowledge that the sun exists. The second is seeing the sun with inner sight, as one sees it with the eyes. The third is when the soul becomes one with the separate intellect, which contains all intelligible forms. There is no sensory example for this, because two things cannot become one in bodily existence.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01293

Immediate knowledge is the knowledge a soul has from the beginning, shared by all people. First principles are also self-evident, but unlike other immediate knowledge, they need no sensation, experience, testimony, or repeated report; they require only an understanding of the terms and their relation.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01294

Imagination is an image that remains in the soul after the thing sensed is gone, whether in sleep or waking life. In our view, these images do not exist in the material world and are not imprinted in a bodily power, as philosophers have often claimed of the back part of the brain. Nor are they separate from the soul in an independent imaginal world, as Illuminationist philosophers hold. They exist in the human soul's own world, joined to it and sustained by it for as long as it preserves them. When the soul turns away from them, they disappear; when it recalls them, they appear again.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01295

The power that perceives imagined forms is itself free of this world, its bodies, and its features. It is one level of the soul, between sensation and intellect. Though the soul is one in its essence, it has different levels, each higher than the one below it, and each belongs to its own world.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01296

Reflection is knowledge reached after much thought. Practical intelligence is the soul's ability to work out what will benefit a person most. This is why the Prophet said: “The wise person is the one who holds himself to account and works for what comes after death.” Nothing a person can gain is better than what comes after death. Experience is knowledge reached through testing and careful examination.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01297

Judgment is turning over premises from which a desired conclusion may follow. The conclusion itself is also sometimes called a judgment. Judgment is to thought as a tool is to a craftsperson. Hence the sayings: “Beware of a hasty opinion,” and “Do not trust an opinion formed in haste.”
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01298

Physiognomy is drawing conclusions about a person's inner character from outward features. The Qur'an alludes to it when it says, “There are signs for those who can read them,” “You will know them by their mark,” and “You will know them by the tone of their speech.” The word originally referred to a predator snatching its prey; physiognomy is like snatching up knowledge. It has two kinds. One comes to a person as an insight whose cause is unknown. This is a kind of inspiration, even revelation, and is what the Prophet meant when he said that there are people in his community who receive inspired thoughts. He also said, “Beware the insight of the believer, for he sees by God's light.” This is called a thought cast into the heart. The other kind is learned: it infers inner character from outward features. Those who know these matters say that in the verse “Is one who stands on clear proof from his Lord, followed by a witness from Him,” the clear proof points to the first kind—the purity of the spirit—while the witness points to the second, reading inner states from outward signs.
Stage Ten: Intellect and What It Understands
passage-en-01299

Here, the same word is used in distinct senses; there is no one shared feature behind all of them. The power to act and the capacity to be affected have no common feature that defines them both. The same holds for forms that make a thing what it is and qualities a thing can have, as will be explained later. Some powers to act may still share a common class.
Notes
passage-en-01301

The Imam gives this account in Al-Mabāḥith al-Mashriqiyya. It explains how the meanings of power are related, but it may not match how ordinary speakers extend a word from one similar thing to another. The word may first have meant the source of strenuous actions. It was then applied to the source of being affected, when being affected was itself difficult. People may have thought of being affected as a kind of action, and of an effect as coming from a power in its source. The word was later extended to the source of both action and being affected, whether or not either was strenuous: people thought that a stronger effect came from a stronger source, so strong and weak effects seemed to share one kind of source. Then they came to think that every effect is present in its power. Fire, for example, contains heat that it passes on to nearby things. The effect was said to exist in the power in an indistinct, unformed way, and in the act in a distinct, formed way. Finally, act came to mean anything that exists in a distinct and definite form, while power meant that same thing without distinction or definite form. On this account, power came to mean the possibility of something existing in the source that brings it about.
Notes
passage-en-01302
“Quality” here is used as a descriptive term: the feature described may be the subject itself, one of its parts, or something outside it.

passage-en-01303

The point is that a line may be able to form the side of a square, or may not—like a curved line. The square is called something that could potentially come from the line, as when a curved line could form a square's side if straightened. Do not take the author's note on Avicenna's The Healing to mean that the line is the potential of the square: there he says that the square is what the line can potentially produce. Here, as in Avicenna's own wording, the square is called the power of the line. This is a separate use of power: it does not mean the source of strenuous action, ability, resistance to being affected, or readiness to become something. A square already contains its side in actuality, so the comparison with possibility is only an analogy. The possibility associated with a square is included in its necessary, actual existence, and is present there in a fuller way. That is why the line's actual presence in the square can be called “power” in this geometric sense. Mathematicians also use “in the power of” when one line's square equals the sum of the squares of two other lines. For example, a line 10 units long is in the power of lines 6 and 8 because 10² = 6² + 8². A line does not fit this usage when its square is not equal to the sum of the other two squares. Here, however, the author and Avicenna mean the familiar square figure.
Notes
passage-en-01304

This note restarts the classification from a broader point of view. Active power may be wholly dominant over all beings. In that case, it is the First Principle, exalted be His glory, whose power embraces all. Or it may be subject in some way and under God's control. If it is independent of matter both in what it is and in what it does, it belongs among the higher beings that do not depend on matter. If it is not, then it may produce one action, and so on.
Notes
passage-en-01305

The wording here is not fully clear. At first it seems to refer to the power to act, but its ending seems to refer to the capacity to be affected, as the phrase “the actual and the possible would be together” suggests. The point holds either way. A particular action comes from outside causes; it does not come from the power alone. Power and action also come in degrees. If this is power to act, it is at a stronger level than the action it produces. If it is the capacity to be affected, the relation is reversed: the actual change is stronger than the capacity to receive it. The note promises to explain this further.
Notes
passage-en-01306

You might object that this argument does not work. It discusses the power to act, not the capacity to be affected, and there is no problem with the power to act existing at the same time as the result it produces. The real problem would be for a thing's readiness to remain once what it was ready for had become actual. The reply is that if the power to act on one particular individual remained after that individual came into being, then, on the recipient's side, the capacity to be affected would remain alongside the actual result. The same thing would then be both still only possible and already actual, which is impossible. This confirms the point: power directed at one particular individual ends when that individual exists, while power directed at an unspecified individual of the same kind remains.
Notes
passage-en-01307

Even more surprising, many later writers, including al-Fakhrī, accepted this explanation and tried to reconcile the two views. They said that those who required power to be present with the action meant a power with all the conditions needed to produce the effect; those who said power came before the action meant a power still missing some of those conditions. The commentator says this confuses two meanings. An animal's ability is a power that comes with the possibility of acting or not acting. That possibility cannot exist at the same time as its full realization. A power with every condition in place is power in another sense.
